hops.afterHeading: Counting inhibitions: the basal ganglia brake
hops.title: The lamprey already has the brake
hops.text: The river lamprey has no jaws, a round sucker for a mouth, and a family line that split from ours more than 500 million years ago. It does not look like a close relative. Yet when a team at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm studied lamprey forebrains, they found striatum, GPi, GPe and STN all in place. Pallidal output neurons held a steady inhibitory brake on motor regions. One striatal route reached the output directly; another detoured through GPe and STN. In a follow-up, drugs that activate dopamine receptors made D1 neurons more excitable and D2 neurons less. The circuit you are counting is very likely older than jaws.

sources.citation: Stephenson-Jones M, Samuelsson E, Ericsson J, Robertson B, Grillner S. Evolutionary conservation of the basal ganglia as a common vertebrate mechanism for action selection. Curr Biol. 2011;21:1081-1091. PMID 21700460.

Ericsson J, Stephenson-Jones M, Perez-Fernandez J, Robertson B, Silberberg G, Grillner S. Dopamine differentially modulates the excitability of striatal neurons of the direct and indirect pathways in lamprey. J Neurosci. 2013;33:8045-8054. PMID 23637194.

hops.afterHeading: Both counts together: silencing the STN
hops.title: How a tremor operation led to stimulating the STN
hops.text: In 1987 a Grenoble team led by neurosurgeon Alim-Louis Benabid was about to destroy a small patch of thalamus to stop a tremor. While testing the target, they noticed that stimulating it at 100 hertz stopped the tremor on its own. A few years later they tried stimulation in the STN, the nucleus the monkey lesion work had pointed to. In a 51-year-old patient with severe Parkinson's disease, 130-hertz stimulation made it easier to start moving, mainly in the limbs on the opposite side. Their 1995 Lancet report on three patients held a twist: in one, stimulation could set off ballism, which stopped when the stimulation was reduced.

sources.citation: Benabid AL, Pollak P, Louveau A, Henry S, de Rougemont J. Combined (thalamotomy and stimulation) stereotactic surgery of the VIM thalamic nucleus for bilateral Parkinson disease. Appl Neurophysiol. 1987;50:344-346. PMID 3329873.
Pollak P, Benabid AL, Gross C, et al. Effets de la stimulation du noyau sous-thalamique dans la maladie de Parkinson. Rev Neurol (Paris). 1993;149:175-176. PMID 8235208.
Limousin P, Pollak P, Benazzouz A, et al. Effect of parkinsonian signs and symptoms of bilateral subthalamic nucleus stimulation. Lancet. 1995;345:91-95. PMID 7815888.
Bergman H, Wichmann T, DeLong MR. Reversal of experimental parkinsonism by lesions of the subthalamic nucleus. Science. 1990;249:1436-1438. PMID 2402638.

hops.afterHeading: Parkinson's and Huntington's through the circuit
hops.title: Dopamine is not simply the pleasure chemical
hops.text: People talk about a "dopamine hit" as if dopamine were bottled joy. Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson tested it in rats. They used 6-hydroxydopamine, a toxin that models Parkinson's disease, to strip dopamine from the striatum and nucleus accumbens, about 99 percent of it in the most depleted rats. They dripped sugar water or bitter quinine into the rats' mouths through a tiny tube and watched their faces. The rats still stuck out their tongues for sugar and gaped at quinine, like normal rats. Berridge and Robinson concluded that dopamine matters for wanting a reward, not for liking it. In the classic circuit, dopamine helps lift the motor brake.

sources.citation: Berridge KC, Robinson TE. What is the role of dopamine in reward: hedonic impact, reward learning, or incentive salience? Brain Res Rev. 1998;28:309-369. PMID 9858756.
Berridge KC, Robinson TE. Liking, wanting, and the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction. Am Psychol. 2016;71:670-679. PMID 27977239.

image.caption: Rats with about 99 percent of striatal dopamine gone still made the usual pleased tongue movements to sugar.
